content: The content provided outlines the development and implementation of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs at both national and healthcare facility levels, emphasizing evidence-based practices to reduce healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and combat antimicrobial resistance (AMR). A previous review conducted by the SIGHT group assessed the quality of evidence using the Integrated Quality Criteria for Review of Multiple Study Designs (ICROMS) scoring system. The updated SIGHT review and a national-level review applied the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) risk of bias criteria. Based on these systematic reviews, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) formulated recommendations using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. In cases where direct, methodologically sound evidence was unavailable, good practice statements were developed to guide interventions. The eight components of IPC programs identified by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2009, along with ten key components from the SIGHT review, served as the foundation for developing these recommendations. The GDG evaluated the relevance of these components alongside new evidence and identified eight core components for IPC programs. Six of these components apply to both national and facility levels, while two are specific to healthcare facilities. The GDG formulated 11 recommendations and three good practice statements, emphasizing that all core components are equally important for establishing and maintaining effective IPC programs. Countries and facilities may prioritize specific components based on their context, achievements, and gaps, with the ultimate goal of implementing a comprehensive approach across all eight components. The successful implementation of these recommendations depends on a robust strategy and a defined process for adaptation and integration into regional, national, and facility-level strategies. The effectiveness of implementation will vary based on existing health systems, available resources, and policies. Support from key stakeholders, partner agencies, and organizations is critical. A separate resource will accompany these guidelines, providing strategies for implementation in resource-limited settings and offering IPC training packages aligned with the core components and good practices. Core Components of IPC Programs 1. IPC Programs: At the healthcare facility level, a dedicated, trained IPC team should be established in every acute care facility to prevent HAIs and combat AMR. The program must have clear objectives based on local epidemiology and risk assessments. A minimum staffing ratio of one full-time infection preventionist per 250 beds is recommended, though a higher ratio (e.g., one per 100 beds) may be necessary due to increasing patient complexity. At the national level, standalone IPC programs with defined objectives, functions, and activities should be established. These programs should align with other national health initiatives and include trained infection preventionists with formal IPC training, allocated time, and authority to implement decisions. A dedicated budget and strong linkages with related programs are essential. 2. IPC Guidelines: Evidence-based IPC guidelines should be developed and implemented to reduce HAIs and AMR. Education and training of healthcare workers on these guidelines, along with monitoring adherence, are critical for successful implementation. Guidelines should be adapted to local conditions for effective uptake. At the national level, developing evidence-based IPC guidelines and implementation strategies is a key function of the national IPC program. Ensuring the necessary infrastructure and supplies to support guideline implementation is also essential. 3. IPC Education and Training: At the facility level, IPC education should be provided to all healthcare workers using participatory, team-based strategies, including bedside and simulation training. This should be part of an overall education strategy, including orientation for new employees and continuous education for existing staff. At the national level, the IPC program should support workforce education and training. National IPC curricula should be developed in collaboration with academic institutions, referencing international standards and adapting them to local needs. 4. Surveillance: Surveillance of HAIs is critical for guiding IPC strategies. Facility-level surveillance should follow national recommendations and provide data on infection incidence, AMR patterns, high-risk populations, and the impact of interventions. Quality microbiology and laboratory capacity are essential for reliable surveillance. At the national level, HAI surveillance systems should support public health capacity building and early outbreak detection. National programs require government support, standardized case definitions, and mechanisms for data analysis and reporting. 5. Multimodal Strategies: At the facility level, IPC activities should use multimodal strategies to improve practices and reduce HAIs and AMR. These strategies should involve organizational culture change and the engagement of champions or role models. At the national level, IPC programs should coordinate and facilitate multimodal strategies nationwide, supported by policies, regulations, and resources from the Ministry of Health. 6. Monitoring and Feedback: At the facility level, regular monitoring and timely feedback on IPC practices should be conducted to prevent HAIs and AMR. Feedback should be shared with all relevant staff and hospital management to drive behavior change and improve care quality. At the national level, a monitoring and evaluation program should assess adherence to IPC standards and track progress toward national goals. Hand hygiene compliance should be a key performance indicator. 7. Workload, Staffing, and Bed Occupancy: Bed occupancy should not exceed the facility's standard capacity, and staffing levels should match patient workload. Adequate spacing between beds is essential to reduce HAI risk. 8. Built Environment, Materials, and Equipment: Patient care should occur in a clean, hygienic environment with adequate water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure and IPC materials. Senior facility managers and local authorities are responsible for maintaining a hygienic environment, supported by national IPC and WASH programs. Materials and equipment for hand hygiene should be readily available at the point of care. Background and Importance of IPC Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are among the most common adverse events in care delivery, posing significant public health challenges due to their impact on morbidity, mortality, and quality of life. However, a large proportion of HAIs are preventable. Strengthening IPC capacity at national and facility levels is essential for resilient health systems, particularly in the context of global public health emergencies and the growing threat of AMR. These guidelines aim to address gaps in international evidence-based recommendations and support countries in developing national action plans to combat AMR and improve patient safety. Target Audience The guidelines are intended for policymakers responsible for establishing and monitoring national IPC programs, as well as healthcare facility managers and IPC teams tasked with implementing IPC practices. The recommendations aim to facilitate evidence-based decision-making and improve IPC capacity at all levels of the health system.
